opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the starting point is to ask what a world model is actually *for*. A lot of the current excitement treats world models as predicting the next video frame, rendering pixels of what the world will look like a second from now. That's impressive, and it's useful for some things like robotics and simulation. But I don't think that's mostly how intelligent agents, humans included, reason about the world.

When you think about what will happen if you knock a glass off the table, you're not mentally rendering every shard at high resolution. You're thinking at a much more abstract level: the glass falls, it breaks, there's water on the floor, someone has to clean it up. Those are semantic abstractions. They're the level at which you can plan, explain, and generalize. Pixel-level prediction spends enormous capacity on details that mostly don't matter for decision-making, like the exact texture of the carpet.

And this is where language comes in, which is not surprising given where I'm coming from. Human language is, in a sense, a giant compressed record of the abstractions people have found useful for describing and reasoning about the world. We have words for objects, events, causes, intentions, and social relationships because those are the joints at which it pays to carve reality. So language gives us an enormously rich, already-learned inventory of semantic abstractions, and it's no accident that large language models picked up a surprising amount of world knowledge just from text.

I wouldn't say language alone is sufficient. There's a lot of spatial, physical, and embodied understanding that's poorly captured in text, and you do need grounding in perception and action. But I think the right architecture has a semantic, symbolic-ish level of representation at its core, connected to perception below it, rather than trying to do everything in a continuous pixel or latent space and hoping abstractions emerge. Abstraction is what makes generalization possible. If your model only knows how the world looks, it has a hard time telling you why things happen or what would happen in a situation it's never seen. If it knows what's going on at a semantic level, it can compose that knowledge in new ways, and that's really the essence of intelligence.

r001.rationale: It describes human language as a compressed record of abstractions people found useful, with words for meaningful aspects of the world.

r002.rationale: It does not compare how much data pixel-based learning requires with learning from text, or claim an orders-of-magnitude difference.

r003.rationale: It contrasts semantic reasoning with rendering every visual detail, but does not say people represent surroundings outside their immediate focus through abstract descriptions.

r004.rationale: It says pixel-level prediction spends capacity on details that do not matter for decisions, but does not connect this to real-time modeling limits.

r005.rationale: It says semantic abstractions help agents plan, but does not specifically connect abstract representations to long-term planning.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd actually push back a little on the framing, because I don't think I'd say semantic abstractions are *the* right representation, full stop. What I'd say is that they're an enormously useful level of description, and that the history of both human cognition and of AI gives us good reason to think so.

Let me start with the obvious observation. Humans don't model the world at the level of pixels or air pressure waves. We model it in terms of objects, agents, events, causes, intentions, goals. When you walk into a kitchen, you don't represent the distribution of photons hitting your retina. You represent that there's a pot on the stove, that it's probably hot, that someone was cooking and may come back. Those are semantic categories. And they're useful precisely because they compress away enormous amounts of irrelevant detail while preserving the things you need to predict and act. That's really the whole point of an abstraction. It's lossy in exactly the right ways.

Now, the reason I think this matters for world models in AI is that there's been a tendency, especially coming out of the video prediction and reinforcement learning communities, to think that a world model should be something like a physics simulator. You predict the next frame, or the next sensory state, and if you do that well enough you've got a world model. And I'm skeptical of that as the primary target, because most of the bits in the next frame are things you don't care about. The exact way the leaves move in the wind is unpredictable and irrelevant. What matters is that the car is going to pull out in front of you. So a model that's optimized for pixel-level reconstruction is spending its capacity on the wrong things.

Language is interesting here because language is, in some sense, humanity's accumulated compression of the world into semantic abstractions. When we say "the cup fell off the table," we've already done the work of carving reality into a cup, a table, a falling event, and an implied causal structure. Thousands of years of human beings deciding what distinctions are worth making are baked into the vocabulary and the grammar. So a model trained on language inherits a huge amount of that abstraction for free. I think that's a big part of why large language models turned out to have more of a world model than many people, including many of my colleagues, expected. It's not that text is a complete description of the world, it obviously isn't. It's that text is already pitched at roughly the right level of abstraction for reasoning and planning.

I should say, this isn't an argument that language is sufficient. There are things about the physical world, about space, about continuous motion, about how objects feel, that are very poorly represented in text, and I think grounding in perception and action is going to matter a lot. But I'd argue the role of perception is to populate and update those semantic abstractions, not to replace them. You see the scene, and what you extract is "there's a cup near the edge," and then your reasoning operates on that.

There's also a more practical argument, which is about compositionality and generalization. Semantic representations compose. If I know what a cup is, and I know what falling is, I can represent a cup falling even if I've never seen that particular cup fall in that particular lighting. Pixel-level or purely sensorimotor representations don't compose nearly as cleanly. And compositionality is what gets you systematic generalization, which is the thing we've always struggled to get out of neural networks. So to the extent you want a world model that can handle novel situations, you want it operating over things that can be recombined.

And finally there's interpretability and communication. If a world model is organized around concepts that line up with human concepts, then we can inspect it, we can correct it, we can tell it things. You can say "actually, that's not a cup, it's a bowl," and that intervention is meaningful. With a representation that's purely latent and continuous, you have no handle to grab onto.

So, to summarize my actual position: I don't think there's one right representation, and I think good systems will have multiple levels, some of them quite low-level and perceptual. But I think the level at which you do reasoning, planning, and learning from instruction should be a semantic, roughly linguistic level, because that's the level at which the world is predictable, compositional, and communicable. And it's not a coincidence that this is also the level that human language settled on.

r001.rationale: The response describes language as humanity’s accumulated compression of the world into semantic abstractions, shaped by people deciding which distinctions matter.

r002.rationale: It criticizes pixel-level reconstruction and says language provides useful abstractions, but does not compare data requirements or claim pixel learning needs orders of magnitude more data.

r003.rationale: It discusses representing a scene with semantic categories, but does not say people use abstract semantic descriptions for visual surroundings outside their immediate focus.

r004.rationale: It argues that abstraction avoids spending model capacity on irrelevant detail, but does not connect semantic abstractions to computational limits of real-time world modeling.

r005.rationale: It says semantic representations support reasoning and planning, but does not specifically argue that long-term planning favors abstract world representations.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the key is that a useful world model has to abstract away from an enormous amount of detail. If you’re thinking about what happens when you put a cup on a table, most of the time you don’t need to represent every pixel or the precise texture of the table. You need objects, their properties, and the relationships between them. Those are semantic abstractions, and they let you make predictions that carry over to situations you haven’t seen before.

Language is interesting here because it gives us a very rich vocabulary for expressing those abstractions: things, actions, intentions, causes. But I wouldn’t say that a world model should consist entirely of language. There are spatial and physical details that are much better represented in other ways. The important thing is having abstractions that connect to perception and action, so you can reason at the level that matters for what you’re trying to do.

r001.rationale: The response says language offers a rich vocabulary for expressing abstractions, but does not identify it as a human-designed representation that already abstracts the world.

r002.rationale: It makes no comparison of the data needed to learn semantic abstractions from pixels versus text.

r003.rationale: It does not describe humans representing surroundings outside their immediate focus through abstract semantic descriptions.

r004.rationale: It does not connect semantic abstractions to the computational limits of real-time world modeling.

r005.rationale: It mentions predictions that generalize to unseen situations, but does not argue that long-term planning favors abstract world representations.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I’d qualify that slightly. I don’t think a world model should consist only of semantic abstractions. If you’re catching a ball, the details of motion and timing matter enormously. You don’t want to replace all of that with a symbolic description of a ball coming toward you.

But abstractions let you capture what persists across different experiences. You can see someone pouring water into a glass from many different viewpoints, with different glasses and different lighting, and understand the same underlying event. A useful world model needs to capture that common structure, rather than treating every visual configuration as something entirely new.

And that’s particularly important for generalization and planning. If I tell you that a glass is cracked, you can reason about whether it will hold water without having to simulate every pixel of the scene. You have concepts for objects, properties, and consequences that you can put together in new ways.

Language gives us a very powerful way of expressing those abstractions, but the abstractions have to connect back to perception and action. So I’d argue for representations at multiple levels: enough detail to stay grounded in the world, and enough abstraction to reason beyond the particular situation you’ve already seen.

r001.rationale: The response says language expresses abstractions, but does not identify language as a human-designed representation that already abstracts the world.

r002.rationale: It makes no comparison of data requirements for learning abstractions from pixels versus text.

r003.rationale: It discusses recognizing events across viewpoints, but not representing surroundings outside immediate focus through abstract semantic descriptions.

r004.rationale: It does not connect semantic abstractions to computational limits in real-time world modeling.

r005.rationale: It links abstractions to planning generally, but does not state that long-term planning favors abstract world representations.
